summary: Defines the multipart/report MIME content type, a general container for mail system reports of any kind. This memo defines its use for delivery status reports, and it is one of four documents describing delivery status notifications. It was replaced by RFC 6522.

plainLanguage.summary: A report email needs a folder that holds both the human-readable note and the machine-readable details. This defines that folder type. It was later replaced by RFC 6522.

questions: how are email bounce messages structured
subtitle: A container for email reports mixing human and machine readable content.

tldr.problem: Email systems need to send reports about delivery failures, processing errors, and other events that affect message handling, but these reports must be understood by both humans and automated systems.
tldr.mechanism: Multipart/Report defines a MIME container with a human-readable explanation, a machine-readable part describing what happened, and optionally the original message or its headers.
tldr.outcome: Systems can now send structured failure reports that humans can understand and applications can parse automatically. It was superseded by RFC 6522 with further refinements.

today: RFC 6522 obsoletes RFC 3462, providing a revised specification for multipart/report.

sections.title: The Multipart/Report Container
sections.content:
RFC 3462 defines the Multipart/Report MIME content type, a container for electronic mail reports of any kind. Although primarily designed for delivery status notifications, it serves as a general family type for all kinds of mail system reports.

The container must always be the top-level MIME type in a report message. This allows mail systems to automatically detect and handle report messages by inspecting the RFC 822 headers. A required parameter, report-type, identifies the kind of report by naming the MIME subtype of the second body part.
sections.plainLanguage: Multipart/Report is like an envelope that holds both a letter explaining what happened and a data sheet with the technical details.

sections.title: The Three-Part Structure
sections.content:
Multipart/Report contains either two or three parts in a fixed order. The first part is a human-readable message in any MIME content type and language. Its purpose is to explain what happened in language a person can understand, even if they cannot interpret the second part.

The second part is machine-parsable, typically a Message/delivery-status body part that describes the reported event in structured form. This part provides details useful to automated systems and experts for diagnosis.

The optional third part contains the original message or just its headers. This helps recipients identify which message the report concerns and aids in troubleshooting. If the message contains binary data and the return path is not binary-safe, only the headers may be returned using the Text/RFC822-Headers content type.
sections.plainLanguage: The report has three slots: first, a friendly explanation a person can read; second, technical data a computer can parse; and third, optionally the original message or its header lines.

sections.title: The Text/RFC822-Headers Content Type
sections.content:
When returning only message headers rather than the full original message, RFC 3462 defines the Text/RFC822-Headers MIME content type. This type specifically labels and returns only the RFC 822 header lines from the failed message.

The headers provide enough information to identify which message prompted the report and enable diagnostics based on the Received header chain. The headers must include all lines before the blank line that separates headers from the message body, including MIME-Version and Content-Headers. Unlike Message/RFC822, this type explicitly indicates that only headers are present, not the complete message.
sections.plainLanguage: When you send back just the address label from the original letter instead of the whole letter, this special type says 'this is just the headers, not the whole message.'

sections.title: Security Issues with Reports
sections.content:
Automated processing of report messages without authentication presents security risks. Forged negative reports can be used for denial-of-service attacks, especially when reports trigger automatic directory or mailing list maintenance. Forged positive delivery reports can deceive senders into believing messages arrived when they did not.

A digital signature covering the entire multipart/report structure could prevent such forgeries, but RFC 3462 does not define a signature scheme; implementers must handle this concern through other means appropriate to their security environment.
sections.plainLanguage: Someone could fake a bounce message to either block important mail or trick you into thinking something was delivered when it wasn't. You need to verify that bounce messages are real.

sections.title: Status and Successors
sections.content: RFC 3462 is a Draft Standard that replaced RFC 1892 with only minor editorial changes. The specification was further refined by RFC 6522, which supersedes it. Related specifications include RFC 5337, which updates this document, and RFC 3464, which defines the Message/delivery-status part used inside multipart/report containers.
sections.plainLanguage: This spec was a minor update to an earlier RFC. Later on, RFC 6522 made it better.
